analysis.investment_thesis: GMDC is a government-owned lignite miner selling an undifferentiated commodity at 36x earnings — precisely the combination of characteristics that destroys long-term capital. There is no durable competitive advantage, returns are below my 15% ROIC threshold, and the valuation assumes a commodity cycle that has already peaked.
key_strengths: Near-zero debt (D/E: 0.04) and INR 119 Cr cash provide balance sheet resilience through commodity downturns
Government mining licenses and resource tenure create a quasi-monopoly on lignite deposits in Gujarat, limiting new entrants
OCF positive all 5 years reviewed, with FY25 operating CF of INR 1,059 Cr showing the business can generate cash at current coal prices
key_risks: Extreme earnings cyclicality: EBITDA swung from INR 84 Cr (FY21) to INR 1,730 Cr (FY23) to INR 984 Cr (FY25) — this is not a predictable earnings machine
No pricing power whatsoever — lignite is a low-grade commodity, and GMDC is a price-taker at the mercy of energy markets
Secularly declining industry: global and Indian energy transition away from thermal coal makes lignite a stranded asset risk over the next decade
red_flags: ROE of only 10.9% — well below the 15% minimum I require; paying 3.48x book for sub-par returns is irrational
INR 355 Cr of 'other income' in FY25 propped up net profit of INR 686 Cr — strip that out and core mining operations earned barely INR 330 Cr, implying true operating P/E closer to 70x
CWIP surged from INR 28 Cr (FY23) to INR 619 Cr (FY25) with capex of INR 644 Cr in FY25 — heavy capital deployment into a sunset industry is deeply concerning
Government (Gujarat state) owns 74%; management incentives are political, not value-creation oriented — a chronic problem for PSU miners
FY24 FCF was negative INR 366 Cr — the business consumed cash in a down year, highlighting how capital-intensive this business truly is
analysis.detailed_analysis:
GMDC embodies every characteristic Munger warns against: it is a commodity business with zero pricing power, managed by government appointees whose incentives are misaligned with minority shareholders, operating in a secularly declining industry, and priced at 36x earnings as if it were a compounding machine. The gross margin of 83% is superficially impressive but collapses to a 13.59% operating margin once mining costs, D&A, and overheads are accounted for — exposing a capital-intensive operation masquerading as a high-margin business. The ROIC story is equally disappointing: ROE of 10.9% and ROCE of 14.1% fall short of the 15% threshold I consider the minimum for a quality business, and these returns were achieved at a cyclical peak. When coal prices normalized in FY21, the company lost money outright (net loss of INR 39 Cr).

Invert the thesis to see the danger clearly: you are paying INR 23,433 Cr of market cap for a business that (a) earned INR 686 Cr net in FY25 but relied on INR 355 Cr of non-operating income to get there, (b) is now deploying INR 619 Cr of capital-in-progress into a commodity facing structural decline as India accelerates its renewable energy buildout, and (c) has demonstrated it can swing to losses in bad years. At EV/EBITDA of 34x, the market is pricing GMDC as a growth compounder — it is nothing of the sort. The only scenario where this works out is a sustained supercycle in lignite/coal prices, which is precisely the kind of macro bet I never make. Pass entirely.
